content: The document provides detailed guidance on various contraceptive methods and their medical eligibility criteria, as established by the World Health Organization (WHO). It includes information on the safety and appropriateness of contraceptive methods in the context of specific health conditions and characteristics. The fifth edition of the Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (MEC) builds upon previous editions, incorporating the latest clinical and epidemiological data to ensure evidence-based recommendations. The contraceptive methods covered in this document include low-dose combined oral contraceptives (COCs), combined patches, combined vaginal rings (CVRs), combined injectable contraceptives (CICs), progestogen-only pills (POPs), depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA), norethisterone enanthate (NET-EN), levonorgestrel (LNG) and etonogestrel (ETG) implants, emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs), copper-bearing intrauterine devices (Cu-IUDs), levonorgestrel-releasing IUDs (LNG-IUDs), copper-IUDs for emergency contraception (E-IUDs), progesterone-releasing vaginal rings (PVRs), barrier methods, fertility awareness-based methods (FABs), lactational amenorrhea method (LAM), coitus interruptus (CI), and both female and male sterilization procedures. For each medical condition or characteristic, contraceptive methods are categorized into one of four numbered categories: 1. A condition for which there is no restriction on the use of the contraceptive method. 2. A condition where the advantages of using the method generally outweigh the theoretical or proven risks. 3. A condition where the theoretical or proven risks usually outweigh the advantages of using the method. 4. A condition that represents an unacceptable health risk if the contraceptive method is used. The document emphasizes that the safety of a contraceptive method should be weighed against the benefits of preventing unintended pregnancy. It also highlights that more than one medical condition may need to be considered together to determine contraceptive eligibility for an individual. The intended audience for this publication includes policymakers, family planning program managers, and the scientific community. The MEC aims to provide guidance to national family planning and reproductive health programs in preparing guidelines for the delivery of contraceptive services. It is not intended to serve as actual guidelines but rather as a reference for interpretation and application at the country and program levels, reflecting the diversity of situations and settings in which contraceptives are provided. The document also acknowledges the contributions of the Guideline Development Group, the Evidence Secretariat, and external peer reviewers in developing these recommendations. WHO convened multiple consultations to finalize the fifth edition, and the recommendations are based on systematic reviews and expert input. The development of this guideline was financially supported by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). The document includes tools and job aids to help providers implement these recommendations in practice. It also outlines the importance of considering individual circumstances, such as age, postpartum status, breastfeeding, history of cardiovascular disease, migraines, liver disease, and other medical conditions, when determining contraceptive eligibility. The guidance is designed to be adaptable to diverse clinical and programmatic settings worldwide.
